tiles.heading: 01 · MALE ABOVE, FEMALE BELOW
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1332) — Compare the two sections of one flowering branch. The Flora describes a hard lower seed-bearing section and an upper pollen-bearing section with crowded spikelet pairs.

LOOK HERE FIRST: trace ONE gamagrass raceme from its narrow upper pollen-bearing pairs to the swollen, jointed lower female section. Actual Uvalde panels 1, 4, 5 and 6 show this architecture, anthers and feathery stigmas. Anthers and stigmas are different organs; an immature green joint is not a ripe grain.
tiles.short: One thick flowering spike carries paired male spikelets ABOVE and single embedded female units BELOW
tiles.status: ACTUAL REPRODUCTIVE PHOTO — NO CALIBRATED DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED CLUMP AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Warm-season perennial with short knotty rhizomes, wide strongly midribbed blades and robust culms. Published ligule commonly ~1–3 mm (Go Botany), ~1–1.5 mm (Tropical Forages), with a ciliolate margin and no auricles. Existing Uvalde rooted-clump photo does NOT expose the rhizome or free ligule margin; photograph a connected blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm ruler.
tiles.short: Broad V-folded leaves, stout perennial base; true ligule is a SHORT fringed membrane
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — ATTACHED RHIZOME AND MEASURED LIGULE

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO SEX-SPECIFIC SPIKELET TYPES
tiles.details: Male spikelets commonly ~6–12 mm in Kew treatments, with local UT glumes ~9 mm (lower) and ~8.5 mm (upper). Female units are embedded; UT gives ~9.5–11 mm including enclosing bracts, while Kew reports ~6–8 mm for its fertile-spikelet concept. These are different measurement conventions, not an exact size cutoff. Count and measure SAME-raceme mature units.
tiles.short: Upper male spikelets are paired; lower female spikelets are solitary inside swollen rachis joints
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SAME-SPIKE MALE/FEMALE PAIR WITH 1-MM SCALE

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMAS AND NO LONG AWN
tiles.details: The upper male region has TWO glumes around staminate floral parts; UT describes male lemma ~6–7 mm. In a female unit the lower outer glume hardens, the upper glume is softer, and a reduced sterile lemma can accompany the fertile lemma (~7–8 mm across treatments) and palea (~5 mm locally). Do not label an exposed anther as an awn, or the entire female bead as one naked seed.
tiles.short: Dissect sex-specific units: outer glumes surround smaller lemma/palea; no conspicuous long lemma awns
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SEPARATED MALE/FEMALE GLUMES AND LEMMAS

tiles.heading: 05 · HARD JOINTS, NOT LOOSE GRAINS
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1332) — Look for the seams between the hard lower joints. The Flora describes this section breaking into bead-like units at maturity.

Mature female joints are commonly ~6–10 mm in published descriptions and disarticulate individually. Uvalde panel 7 shows hardening attached tan joints, NOT a separated caryopsis or measured detached joint. Photograph naturally detached beads from both ends and dissect one to expose the enclosed fruit at 1-mm scale.
tiles.short: Mature lower female rachis breaks into beadlike units containing the true fruit
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — DETACHED RIPE JOINT AND ENCLOSED CARYOPSIS

tiles.heading: 06 · PROTECT NATIVE LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Big bluestem has thin turkey-foot rays with sessile/pedicelled units, not a thick female bead chain. Native Indiangrass has a branched golden panicle with twisted lemma awns. Introduced Johnsongrass has an open branching panicle of small spikelets. Corn bears tassels and ears in separate inflorescences, not both sexes along one gamagrass spike. Confirm mature anatomy before treatment.
tiles.short: Gamagrass has a thick sex-divided axis; bluestem, Indiangrass and Johnsongrass do not
tiles.status: FIELD COMPARISON — MATCHED SCALE LOOK-ALIKE PHOTOS NEEDED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FIRST: find the unusually broad arching leaves forming a large robust warm-season clump. NEXT, look for the CORN-RELATIVE flowering head: one to a few thick fingerlike spikes. On a SINGLE spike, the upper region carries closely packed paired MALE (staminate) spikelets and the LOWER portion carries enlarged one-by-one FEMALE (pistillate) joints. Look for conspicuous feathery purple stigmas emerging below (these are NOT anthers). At maturity the lower joints become hard and break apart separately like small beads. Two actual archived source-labelled photographs now show flowering axis and leafy tuft. Don't identify this grass from leaves alone; distinguish Johnsongrass's airy branching seedhead, Indiangrass's feathery branched panicle and big bluestem's separate skinny turkey-foot rays.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Find the very broad blades and massive arching green bunch shown in photo 2. Look carefully for a strong central midrib; a single big leaf is NOT enough to identify gamagrass.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Warm-season perennial with short knotty rhizomes, wide strongly midribbed blades and robust culms. Published ligule commonly ~1–3 mm (Go Botany), ~1–1.5 mm (Tropical Forages), with a ciliolate margin and no auricles. Existing Uvalde rooted-clump photo does NOT expose the rhizome or free ligule margin; photograph a connected blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Male spikelets commonly ~6–12 mm in Kew treatments, with local UT glumes ~9 mm (lower) and ~8.5 mm (upper). Female units are embedded; UT gives ~9.5–11 mm including enclosing bracts, while Kew reports ~6–8 mm for its fertile-spikelet concept. These are different measurement conventions, not an exact size cutoff. Count and measure SAME-raceme mature units.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: MOST IMPORTANT: One Tripsacum flower axis has a paired staminate (male) upper portion and a much thicker jointed pistillate (female) lower portion, with showy feathery stigmas sometimes visible; mature female joints break apart individually. Big bluestem (Andropogon gerardii) may also carry 2–6 separated turkey-foot racemes but those are SLENDER and have sessile/pedicelled bisexual/floret patterns instead of large jointed female beads. Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans) makes a soft, BRANCHED and awned golden panicle, not a thick bead-jointed axis. Invasive Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) has broad leaves but a many-branched loose panicle of small spikelets, not the conspicuous male-over-female gamagrass axis. Cultivated corn (Zea mays) is also a monoecious relative but separates male tassel and female ear into DIFFERENT inflorescences; Tripsacum has both on the same spike. Do not count immature green female joints as mature shattering seeds.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: WHOLE CLUMP → thick terminal spikes → pollen anthers on UPPER male section → feathery stigmas and enlarging joints on LOWER female section → TAN BEADLIKE ripe joints. Different photos document these stages; do not assume all are the same individual.
safety_note: Spelling: Tripsacum dactyloides. Ripe hard female joints, actual anthers and rhizomes are NOT shown in current two physical local-source photos; do not put anatomically incorrect arrows onto leaves or immature fruits. CC0 source metadata originally recorded, exact GBIF rights currently not reachable; provisional photo/source QA preserved. The five new Jim Conrad Uvalde originals are PUBLIC DOMAIN with page-specific original-author context; direct URLs are external and may not always display on Pages. Do not count as archived bytes. The updated feature indices reference seven current teaching panels.
field_rule: Tripsacum genus clue = thick SAME spike with male region ABOVE and enlarged female beadlike lower joints BELOW. For exact species, verify a mature specimen; lookalike silhouettes and leaf width alone do not prove it.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
